source.title: In-Context Linear Regression Demystified: Training Dynamics and Mechanistic Interpretability of Multi-Head Softmax Attention
source.authors: Jianliang He; Xintian Pan; Siyu Chen; Zhuoran Yang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports superposition among attention heads in a synthetic multi-task regression model, but does not measure neuron polysemanticity or test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The reported results about learned KQ/OV circuits, alternative attention activations, and head-level task superposition do not measure neuron responses or meanings. The head-level superposition result is recorded as a related but different construct. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study trains one-layer multi-head softmax attention on synthetic in-context linear regression and analyses KQ/OV circuits. It has no MLP neurons, no image or language inputs, and no measure of individual units responding to unrelated inputs. Its 'superposition' result concerns attention heads serving two regression tasks (H=3, N=2), which is related to V3 but is a different unit (heads) and a different construct (task allocation, not polysemantic neurons). It neither tests nor uses neuron polysemanticity.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that with limited heads (2<H<2N) individual heads encode multiple tasks via superposition. In the H=3, N=2 case this recovers the two task-specific debiased GD predictors. They call the general case future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes trained synthetic attention circuits and task allocation; it does not apply neuron activation visualization or an intervention on neuron meanings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported multi-task head patterns depend on the head-to-task ratio: the paper distinguishes H=1, H=2, H≥2N, and 2<H<2N regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: With H=3 heads and N=2 overlapping regression tasks, all heads contribute to both tasks. Head 3 acts as a negative head for Task 1 and a positive head for Task 2. The model still implements two task-specific debiased GD predictors. With H>=2N, heads specialise per task instead.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When attention heads are fewer than twice the number of tasks, trained transformers superpose several task computations within individual heads; with enough heads, heads become task-specific.

record.problems: The relevant result is a synthetic, small-scale setting: the detailed superposition example uses two tasks and three heads. The authors describe broader behavior for 2<H<2N as varying across runs and present generalization of the phenomenon as a belief for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No neuron-level results are reported. Other experiments, including activation-function comparisons and head-count comparisons, do not measure neuron polysemanticity and are not rows for the listed versions.

untested.parts: No vision models or neurons studied.
No language-model MLP neurons or token/context responses.
No neuron-level test of whether polysemanticity stems from packing more sparse features than neurons. Only the head-level analogue appears.
No neuron polysemanticity measured under initialization, regularization or noise.
Alternative attention activations (1+x, (1+Cx)^2, 1+tanh) are compared on learned weights and ICL loss only, not on the share of polysemantic units.
No polysemanticity measurement or scoring comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is upheld. The capacity-dependent head specialisation versus superposition (H>=2N vs 2<H<2N) loosely parallels V3's logic. However, it concerns attention heads in a toy regression model, so it is recorded only under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: No vision model or image-responsive neurons are studied.
No language model neurons or token/context response rates are studied.
The study does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by feature capacity pressure. Its related result concerns attention heads representing multiple tasks.
No neuron-level polysemanticity under initialization, regularization, or training noise is measured.
Alternative attention activations are tested for regression performance and attention-weight patterns, not for the share of polysemantic neurons.
No neuron explanations or shared-feature interpretations are examined.
No neuron polysemanticity measurement or explanation-scoring method is compared.

rows.subject: three-head attention model
rows.operation_detail: Inspected learned attention KQ and OV patterns in multi-task linear regression.
rows.measure: Head-level task superposition in learned parameters and resulting predictor
rows.value: All three heads contribute to both tasks; Head 3 is negative for Task 1 and positive for Task 2. The authors report that the model implements the two independent debiased GD predictors through superposition.
rows.note: This is superposition across attention heads and regression tasks, not evidence about individual neurons or unrelated input meanings.
rows.check: Head-level superposition across two regression tasks, not neuron polysemanticity. 'Observed' describes the head-superposition pattern, not any claim version. It is a single run; the authors say the pattern varies across runs when 2<H<2N. Correctly unlinked.

relation.reason: Invokes superposition to describe heads serving two tasks but neither tests nor uses the neuron claim; discusses fits (cites_only also defensible).

tranche.reason: Attention-head task superposition in synthetic in-context linear regression; no neurons, no unrelated inputs, no polysemanticity measure; Elhage et al. only cited for the term.

source_check.notes: Not evidence on polysemantic neurons: 'superposition' here is attention heads serving two regression tasks (one toy run, H=3, N=2), and the authors say patterns vary across repeated runs and leave the general case to future work. The paper contradicts itself: Sec 5.4 says the shared head is positive for task one and negative for task two, but Appendix A.3 and Fig 19 say Head 3 is negative for Task 1 and positive for Task 2. The row follows the appendix.
